HCBCOGN312.topics: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.contribution: develops research and writing methods for constructing evidence-based histories of art
MCCHEAM316.topics: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.

MCCLITR111.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
MCCLITR111.contribution: introduces close reading, literary interpretation and critical analysis of cultural texts
MCCLITR111.topics: Definitions and value of literature; Literary genre and originality; Story, plot and narrative structure; Character, setting and point of view; Symbolism and allegory; Style, tone, humour and irony; Graphic fiction and microfiction; Creative nonfiction and memoir; Children's literature; Poetic language, imagery, sound and form; Drama and tragedy; Film adaptation
MCCLITR111.methods: Close reading; Formalist literary analysis; Narrative analysis; Poetic and dramatic analysis; Critical-source integration; Literary essay and review construction

MCCLITR112.name: Great Literary Works
MCCLITR112.contribution: examines major literary works across periods and cultures through close reading and comparative interpretation
MCCLITR112.topics: Literature, canon and world literature; Epic and heroism; Tragedy, fate and identity; Autobiography and memory; Framed storytelling and narrative power; Gender and agency; Essay and philosophical tale; Satire and irony; Colonialism and its critique; Modernist narration and subjectivity; Alienation and family; Art, sexuality and civilization; Magical realism
MCCLITR112.methods: Close literary reading; Formalist analysis of genre, theme and technique; Comparative textual interpretation; Narrative analysis; Critical-source interpretation and integration

MCCLITR212.name: Life & Travel Writing
MCCLITR212.contribution: Examines how life writing constructs identity, memory and experience.
MCCLITR212.topics: Autobiography and memoir culture; Fact, fiction and autobiographical truth; Autobiographical pact; Self and multiple identities; Individual and collective memory; Experience, embodiment and agency; Ethics and traumatic memory; Grief and disability narratives; Popular memoir and narrative technique; Digital self-presentation; Travel and spiritual self-fashioning; Migration, language and cultural identity
MCCLITR212.methods: Close life-narrative analysis; Smith and Watson's strategies for reading life narratives; Theory-guided analysis of memory, identity, embodiment and agency; Comparative textual and contextual interpretation; Structured autobiographical creative writing

MCCMEDI311.name: Media & Race
MCCMEDI311.contribution: analyses how media represent and construct race, power and identity
MCCMEDI311.topics: Racial construction and whiteness; Media, power and representation; Leisure, tourism and racial identity; Crime, punishment and the racialized body; Asian-American exclusion; Japanese-American incarceration; Childhood and youth; Marginalized and Indigenous storytelling; Racial extremism and propaganda; Alienation and community; Food, environment and cultural nourishment; Afrofuturism and Indigenous futurisms
MCCMEDI311.methods: Participant observation; Archival primary-source research; Historical media analysis; Documentary podcast research, scripting and audio production; Photo/Voice photography and audio narrative; Cross-cultural interpretive reflection

MCCMEDI312.name: The Documentary
MCCMEDI312.contribution: examines documentary form, evidence and representation through critical and creative analysis
MCCMEDI312.topics: Documentary definition, modes and ethics; Early documentary and city symphonies; Soviet filmmaking; European documentary traditions; Direct cinema and cinéma vérité; Audio and public-affairs documentary; Propaganda and advocacy; Historical and ethnographic documentary; Nature documentary; Mockumentary; Interactive and autobiographical documentary; Documentary aesthetics
MCCMEDI312.methods: Critical documentary analysis; Historical and contextual film comparison; Documentary research and interviewing; Script, storyboard and shot-list development; Preproduction planning; Documentary filming and postproduction; Reflective evaluation of production practice

analysis: Society, culture and science uses economics, politics, sociology, history and documentary to examine institutions and representation, and ecology, governance and health psychology to add environmental and behavioural perspectives. Philosophy contributes normative reasoning and theories of emotion; qualitative methods and statistics offer complementary evidence skills. The power and culture alternative studies authority, inequality and identity via law, comparative politics, conflict, history, art, literature, sociology and media. Climate communication contributes analysis of how public arguments are constructed, not natural science. The life, mind and health alternative builds on cells and molecular processes, physiology, neurobiology and brain and behaviour, progressing to laboratory work, perception, epidemiology, pharmacology, clinical psychology, disease mechanisms and research synthesis. Description-only Psycholinguistics and Perception & Action support cognitive and language breadth. Writing Art’s Histories and Researching the American Century likewise supply substantive humanities inquiry on their descriptions. Psycholinguistics is offered only in spring 2027, so it follows the first-term Brain & Behavior gateway in that term. The resulting schedule uses psychopathology before psychodiagnostics and cell biology before molecular pathology. Pairwise course differences verify distinctness. The environment direction is credible but has substantial coverage in the broad option; the separate economics and quantitative science directions have generator support and remain outside the three-option ceiling. Several Humanities topics are represented through adjacent forms of cultural analysis, without implying a dedicated China Studies, performance or religious studies sequence. The Academic Core and PPD share research and argumentation work. Research in Practice and Research Methods & Statistics share empirical design and statistical analysis. Qualitative Research Methodology matches one permitted Social Sciences methods direction. Historical research and meta-analysis remain separate from the named Humanities methods requirement and the UCU thesis. The optional 15 EC UCR row is comparison-only.
